**Melb Cafe/Bakery Profiles for Mid Year Wraps**

** **

**Daybaker**

*An Abbotsford bakery that takes quality over
quantity seriously.*

The first thing to
know about Daybaker is that it’s not trying to do everything. There’s no
sprawling menu, no sourdough program, no all-day offering stretching into the
evening. There are no T-shirts for sale, no take-home pantry staples. Instead,
Charlie Duffy’s (Tivoli Road Bakery and Small Batch) Abbotsford bakery is
built around a single idea: do a small number of things extremely well. 

The menu shows off
his signature style with a core trio that anchors the daily offering: a plain
croissant, a chocolate wattleseed version, and a savoury option. 

Alongside those, a
changing set of pastries will shift with the seasons, including a mixture of
new creations and past Small Batch customer favourites, such as Duffy’s pear
and Geraldton wax danish, all showcasing local produce.

Beyond pastry, the
offering is just as restrained. Lunch is built around Roman-style pizzas and a
couple of sandwiches with fillings that will change often. The concise coffee
program follows suit.

 

**Time After Time**

*A bakery cafe tying together influences from Seoul
and Melbourne*

The relatively
out-there charcoal croissants draw crowds at this CBD bakery. The inky-black
pastries are inspired by popular viennoiseries found in Seoul, where chef and
owner Mino Han runs four pizza shops and Melbourne-style brunch cafe Ummd.
The charcoal is mostly used for aesthetics, with Han taking inspiration from
Korean cafes such as Gentle Monster’s dessert brand Nudake.

A
Melbourne-brunch-inspired charcoal croissant topped with ricotta, berry coulis,
fresh figs and honey is the runaway hit. It’s joined by a matcha-topped
charcoal croissant with custard and shards of matcha butter, and an equally
dramatic black cocoa version. 

There’s coffee and
matcha, but the drink to order is the Time Traveller: a cold-filter coffee
shaken over ice with cream and orange zest. Enjoy one on a laneway stool in
true Melbourne fashion.

* *

** **

**Tatik’s Delights**

*This Southbank cafe bakes Armenian layer cake using
a generations-old family recipe.*

Layers appear
across many Armenian desserts. At Tatik’s you’ll find Armenian napoleons of
house-made puff pastry layered with cream, plus tall caramel wafers – delicate
biscuits, piled high with caramel and walnuts between each. They’re all the
works of co-owners Nawid Fayazi and Aisha Fayazi.

At Tatik’s
Delights, the showstopper is the medovik, or honey cake. It’s made using a
family recipe passed down from Aisha’s tatik (“grandmother” in Armenian). It’s
a labour of love, taking 24 hours to make. Thin sheets of honey biscuit are
baked until crisp, then layered with sweet cream, iced again and finished with
crushed biscuit crumbs. Left to rest overnight, the cream softens each layer
into something closer to sponge cake. 

The space wasn’t
intended as a retail venue. The couple secured it as a commercial kitchen for
their wholesale and catering business, which began in 2024. Inside, bench
seating lines one wall, with several tables outside. 

* *

**Matcha Mate Collingwood**

*A permanent home in Collingwood for a successful
CBD matcha pop-up*

This Collingwood
cafe was originally intended to be a showroom for Matcha Mate’s products, but
there was no stopping hordes of people from showing up for hand-whisked
drinks. Now the team is constantly whisking away, swirling mounds of
matcha cream on top of iced drinks. 

Much like going to
a specialty coffee shop and choosing your beans, here you can pick from seven
different matcha blends. Each, alongside two varieties of hojicha, is available
for purchase from the retail section at the front of the store. Gone are the days
of blind-buying Matcha Mate products – now you can sample each one in an
expertly prepared drink.

There’s also a
rotation of specialty drinks and desserts that change with the seasons. The
space itself is pretty bare-bones and a little industrial, but it’s a stage to
let the drinks do the talking.

* *

**Interlude**

*A CBD cafe and bakery that specialises in Chinese
and Japanese teas.*

Interlude
specialises in Chinese and Japanese teas. It’s run by Sean Then, who also
operates North Melbourne specialty coffee shop Cafe Tomi and Bar Kaeru, a CBD saké spot. For Then, tea was the
logical next step.

On any given day,
there are about five different special tea drinks, three cold brew teas and
more than 20 unique hot teas on offer. Teas include oolong, green, black and
red teas from China and Japan. 

The food menu is
made up predominantly of danishes. Savoury numbers include chorizo and cheddar,
and a corn cheese danish. Plus, there are seasonal, fruitier numbers such as a
raspberry danish and a fig option.

True to its name,
the intention at Interlude is to allow people a quiet moment in Melbourne’s
bustling CBD. There’s an artificial skylight, which, alongside the tiled
flooring, is designed to help people feel more connected to nature. 

* *

**Patricia Lonsdale Street**

*A Melbourne coffee institution’s second, larger
outpost.*

This is the second
outpost for Melbourne coffee institution Patricia. After 15 years on Little
William Street, this roomier site opened on Lonsdale Street. In it, only
pour-over coffee has been added, proving good hospitality is timeless.

The second cafe
gives visitors more room to move. Patricia Lonsdale keeps a familiar bar-style
layout, but adds an adjoining room designed to feel a little like standing
around a kitchen bench. It’s recognisably Patricia, though less compressed,
with the kind of warmth that suits a longer pause rather than a quick
in-and-out coffee run between meetings.

The larger space
has also brought back single-serve pour-over coffee, which disappeared from the
original site in the early days. Little William Street still focuses on
batch-brewed filter, but Lonsdale Street can showcase other coffees one cup at
a time.

The fit-out comes
from Hecker Guthrie, led by Samuel McIntyre, a former Patricia staff member.
Builders Westmark Building Group, alongside Andy Ryan and Illogical Study on
joinery and fabrication, helped shape the heritage listed space around the
peculiar character of the old building.

* *

**Bobby Stop Stealing Our Camping Chairs**

*A Southern Cross cafe that aims to do the opposite
of every other in Melbourne.*

When you enter
Bobby Stop Stealing Our Camping Chairs – Bobby, for short – you could be
greeted by a live band, art installation or DJ. Or even co-owners Michael Teng
and Young Lee walking around the counter to dap you up like an old friend. The
chaos is by design, although there’s nothing contrived about it. 

The concept was
also shaped by necessity: Bobby sits in a tiny space wedged into a corner of
Southern Cross Station with space for one bench inside and a handful of camping
chairs on the footpath. Once the pair decided to open a cafe, they adopted
one underlying ethos: do the opposite of every cafe in Melbourne. And it starts
with the cheap coffee and matcha.

The cafe’s chaos
extends to its social media. Teng and Lee’s most popular posts are videos
captured on their doorbell camera, where passers-by are encouraged to leave a
video note. And from the beginning, the pair agreed that the venue name should
be as long as possible “so that it looks ridiculous on Google Maps”. All of
these choices are designed to make you pause for a moment to take stock of what
you’re looking at.
